One case the e2e never exercises, for the person rather than another round: dragging a node while a step's inspector is open. That is the only time the app hands React Flow a node with `selected: true`. From what I remember of React Flow's drag code, it clears that selection before it picks what to drag, so I expect it to work. I could not read the library source or open a browser to confirm it.

findings.what: The ask was to drag anything, with the right-hand side of the dragged node following and the left staying. That rule is applied to steps only. A card that other runs wait on, joined by the `after` edges the floor draws, moves alone with its own steps. In the e2e's seed, dragging `Lay the diamond top` leaves `One side, shipped`, `The other side, still running` and `The diamond bottom` where they were, and dragging `Called off` leaves `Waits on a called-off run`. The edges stretch across the floor. The hint text admits the asymmetry: `drag to arrange, a step with what follows it`. A card dragged should take the cards that wait on it, directly or through others, by as far, and leave the cards it waits on. It needs a pure function beside `followersOf`, a unit test, and an e2e drag of a card in the seed's diamond that checks what follows and what stays.

`spanOf` claims cells only to the right of the card and below its top. A step dropped left of its card or above it lands on whatever card is there, and nothing moves aside. The step sits on top of that card in this visit and the next, since the move is saved. The comment records this as a choice, and the e2e only checks a drop to the right and down. This is for the person who decides whether a run should claim the cells its steps reach in every direction. It is not required for the round.

In factory-step-dropped-light.png and factory-next-visit-light.png, after the step is dropped, `Read the plan first` is moved into the cell under `What it cost` and covers its bottom edge. The two cards read as one at the left of the floor, around y 355 to 365. Only light pictures of this state were given. The cause is not in this diff. That seeded card, with four steps and an ask, is drawn about 232 px tall in a 220 px cell (`CELL_HEIGHT`), so any card placed under it overlaps. The step drop only made the floor place one there. This is for a person, not for this round.

reviews.summary: The step drag is sound: followers are the steps that wait on the dragged one, the rest stay, moves persist and reset, the uncached test run and the typecheck (replayed from turbo's cache) pass, and both themes read well. The pages were judged from implement's seven screenshots only, because serving the app is denied in this mode and nothing was pressed in a browser. One part of the ask is not done: a card dragged does not take along the cards that wait on it, so I ask for another round on that.

findings.what: *What it leaves* does not record a board disagreement that item 4 introduces. Take a run at its ending's gate whose result a person merged by hand. The api's `decisionOf` (apps/api/src/app.ts:1320-1322) now returns `shipped — <branch> is already on main`. But the api calls `listing` with no standings (app.ts:722), so `waitingOnYou` still contains `ship`, and `needsOf` (app.ts:855-859) still offers `approve ship`. Pressing that Approve button reaches the package's `approve()` and gets the new refusal as a 422. So the run page says the run has shipped and, beside that, asks the person to approve a step whose approval is refused. The counts bullet above presents the api's `decision` change as agreeing with `wf decide`; it should also say that the board's listing and its Approve button do not agree yet. That fits item 5's list of what the board cannot show.

'An approval given before the hand merge still files ship … The window is one pass' is only true when nothing holds the checkout. If the approved ending is waiting on the checkout because another run's ship is in it (`heldByCheckout`), the window lasts as long as that run's session holds the checkout. During that time the approved ending also keeps its claim on the checkout (`mainClaim`) and holds other runs' endings back, only to be filed later with nothing to merge and sign off blocked. The sentence should say 'one pass, or as long as the checkout holds it'.

reviews.summary: I reviewed all eight commits against the five items and the three round-1 replies. All five items are done and tested, and the three replies hold up in the code: `decision` now reads a hand-merged run as shipped, so a child started `--after` it starts; `wf decide` and `wf rm` agree with `wf ls`; and the deny list includes `git pull` and `git restore`, with each rule tested to refuse. `npx turbo run test --force` passed in all 4 packages, and `npm run typecheck` is clean (turbo replayed it from cache). Two small gaps remain, both in features.md's *What it leaves* and neither worth another round: a new disagreement on the board is not recorded, and one of the recorded windows is described as shorter than it can be.

findings.what: A child run waits for ever on a hand-merged parent. A run started with `wf start --after P` starts only when P's `decision` is `shipped`, and `decision` never calls a run shipped while its ending waits at its gate (`awaitingApproval` guard around line 3077; pinned by run.test.ts "a run at its ending step's gate is never shipped … whatever git says"). Before this change, a person whose parent's result was merged by hand could `wf approve P ship`: ship ran, found the branch already merged and signed off, ship was no longer `awaiting approval`, the branch was on the base with commits past it, and P read `shipped`, so the child started. Now `approvalRefusal` refuses that approval and its only suggestion is `wf cancel P`. A cancelled run never ships, so the child's `wf decide` says 'P was cancelled … yours to resolve: wf cancel <child>, or start the work again without --after P'. The refusal's 'Nothing waits on you' is false whenever a run waits on P. Either let an ending that has not run, whose result git has with commits past the base, read as shipped, or leave the gate approvable when a run waits on it (and word the refusal and note accordingly). No test covers a child of a hand-merged parent.

`wf decide P` for a run at ship's gate whose branch was merged by hand still prints 'AWAITING APPROVAL, waiting on you: ship — this workflow's ending, at its gate: nothing of it has run, and your approval is what runs it', a few lines above 'branch wf/…/implement is on main'. At the same moment `wf ls` says nothing waits on you and `wf approve P ship` is refused. That is the same kind of disagreement item 3 fixed (a screen offering a command the verb refuses). The CLI already has the branch standings in hand (line 732), so it can leave such an ending out of `unrun` and print the on-base line and `wf cancel` (or whatever finding 1 settles on) without touching `decision`'s kind. ship.test.ts calls `decide` only after the cancel, so nothing tests this screen before it.

The frontmatter comment and both READMEs say the deny list covers 'everything that moves or throws away what is in a person's checkout', but two ordinary commands, not alternate spellings, are not denied. `git pull` fetches and merges into the person's checkout, and `git pull . wf/<run>/implement` merges a run's result branch, which is the one act this fence exists to stop. `git restore <path>` throws away uncommitted work exactly as `git checkout -- <path>` does, and that one is denied. Add `Bash(git pull:*)` and `Bash(git restore:*)`, with the matching entries in supervisor.test.ts's GIT_DENIED, or narrow the claim.

reviews.summary: Reviewed the five commits against 242f9b1. Items 1, 2, 3 and 5 do what was asked; `npx turbo run test --force` passes in all 4 packages and typecheck is clean. Item 4 has a regression: a run started `--after` a parent whose result was merged by hand at ship's gate can never start, because the approval is refused and the only exit offered (`wf cancel`) makes the parent never ship. `wf decide` also still says 'waiting on you: ship' while `wf ls` says nothing waits.

findings.what: Round totals group every task by `roundIn` of its own step's record (line 2288), and a step outside the loop is always round 1. Take `implement ⇄ review → ship` (a shape the package supports: run.test.ts:1329 has `ship, after the loop`). When the loop goes three rounds, ship is filed after round 3 but counted in round 1's total. So round 1's `ran` includes ship's run time, and round 1's `wall` runs from implement's first filing to ship's end, which is the whole run. `wf decide` prints that as `round 1 ... wall <the run's wall>`, and the run page's tfoot shows the same. A `plan` step before the loop (the shipped `dev-planned`) is also added to round 1, which makes round 1 look slower than later rounds. Only steps in a loop's span (`loopSpan`) should count toward a round's total. Steps outside it count in the run's total alone, or in a row of their own. There is no test with a step outside the loop in `timeline`'s round totals.

`takenBackBy` compares an MCP allow with a deny only when the words are identical, because `ruleOf` returns null for any `mcp__…` name. A settings allow `mcp__fixture__echo` with a deny `mcp__fixture` or `mcp__fixture__*` (from the settings or a step's `disallow:`) stays in `allowed.rules`. For a step not in dontAsk, the page lists `mcp__fixture__echo` under "Allowed without asking", while the same step's MCP tools row strikes `echo` as denied (`denyingRule` does match whole-server denies). It is also missing from `takenBack`. The last round's reply said a deny now takes back every allow whose calls it matches, but that covers Bash only. The fix is to test MCP allows with `denyingRule`'s server / `__*` rule. No test covers a whole-server deny against a single-tool MCP allow.

reviews.summary: I reviewed all six commits against 08bef91, re-checked the three fixes from the last round, and looked at the e2e screenshots of the run, Capabilities and Workflows pages in both themes. The three fixes hold, and a full uncached parallel `npx turbo run test --force` and `npm run typecheck` both pass. I found two remaining wrong results: round totals put steps outside a loop into round 1, and a server-wide MCP deny does not take back an MCP allow.

findings.what: For a `dontAsk` step the page says "In dontAsk, a command no rule allows is denied without a prompt. The settings allow it:" and lists only the settings' Bash allows. For this repo's review steps (dev, dev-build, dev-planned, ui) and dev-planned's plan step, that list is `npm test`, `npm run typecheck`, the `git diff/log/show/status` rules and so on. That is not all such a step runs. Claude Code runs a built-in set of read-only commands (`ls`, `cat`, `grep`, `find`, `head`, `tail`, `wc`, `diff`, read-only `git`) without a prompt in every mode (code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions, "Read-only commands"). This review session measured it: running in `dontAsk` under this repo's settings, `cat`, `ls`, `grep` and `head` ran with no allow rule, while `node -e` and a playwright MCP call were denied. So the MCP marking is right, but the Bash sentence is false: the reviewer can read any file with `cat` or `grep` while the page says it can run only the listed commands. The test at apps/api/test/capabilities.test.ts:460 checks only the settings' allows, so it passes either way. Fix: add "of the commands that ask" to the sentence, or carry the read-only set as dated data beside MEASURED_TOOLS.

reviews.summary: I reviewed all seven commits against items 11–15. Both round-3 fixes hold. A round's total now counts only the steps inside its loop, with separate totals for each loop. And a deny of a whole MCP server now takes back the allows for its tools, matching the tools row. Both are covered by tests that make them refuse. `npx turbo run test --force` passed with the packages in parallel (4 of 4); I ran it once, not three times. `npm run typecheck` passed, but turbo replayed it from cache. The e2e screenshots were taken after the last commit: the loop run shows round 1–3 and run totals, and the Capabilities page shows each step in the dark theme. One finding is left, for a person to weigh, and it is not worth another round: the page's `dontAsk` Bash sentence overstates what is refused.

findings.what:
A deny cancels an allow only when the two rules are word for word the same. A broader deny does not cancel a narrower allow. Example: a step with `disallow: Bash(npm run:*)` under settings that allow `Bash(npm run build)` still gets `npm run build` in `allowed.bash`. The page then lists it under "Bash it may run", although Claude Code denies that command. The same happens with a settings deny of `Bash(git:*)` and an allow of `Bash(git diff:*)`. The REFUSED test only uses an exact-words deny (`Bash(npm run build)` against `Bash(npm run build)`), so the prefix case is untested. Fix: a deny `Bash(

:*)` should also cancel any allow `Bash(

…)`, with a test that fails without it.

`allowed.bash` is built from the settings' allow rules without checking whether the step has Bash at all. A `dontAsk` step with `tools: Read, Grep`, or with `disallow: Bash`, has no Bash tool (`tools.names` has no `Bash`). Yet the page (capabilities.tsx:347) still shows "Bash it may run: npm test, git diff:*". No test covers a dontAsk step without Bash. Fix: when Bash is not among the step's tools, show no commands and say why, and add a test that fails without that.

`MEASURED_TOOLS.tools` includes `Edit` and `Write`, but the plan's record of what was measured ("what a worker gets, measured") never names them. The code comment admits they were added because every implement step edits with them. `Bash`, `Glob`, `Grep`, `Read` and `Skill` are also carried over from the fenced reviewer, not from the unfenced measurement. The page still shows the whole list as "Claude Code's own set, as measured on 2026-09-14 with 2.1.270", so it claims a measurement for tools that weren't measured. Fix: mark the inferred entries separately on the data and the page, or leave them out.

reviews.summary: I read all five commits against 08bef91. `npx turbo run test --force` passed in parallel with nothing cached, and `npm run typecheck` passed from turbo's cache, which is valid for unchanged inputs. I did not run the build or the e2e, as the brief says. Items 11, 12, 13 and 15 do what was asked and have refusal tests. Item 14's Capabilities page claims more than a step can do in two small cases, and labels two tools as measured that nobody measured, so I'm asking for one more round.

findings.what: The README says as fact that "A `view` saw the session listed final thirty seconds before its `StructuredOutput`", and the runner.ts comment at line 379 says the same ("some thirty seconds before"). Nobody recorded that: open-issues.md (around line 278) says the pin was taken between 22:53:25.9Z and 22:53:50.4Z, "at least ten seconds before the statement", and calls it "the reading the evidence allows, not a measurement". The request said the cause is not known and asked to say only what the code allows. As written, a reader of the README or the code takes an unconfirmed guess, with a made-up number, as the known cause, and may stop looking at the other ways a final sighting reaches the runner. The wording should match open-issues: the code allows this, and it was not observed.

The final usage assertion, 'only the responses since its own start', expects {turns 2, toolCalls 2, inputTokens 200, outputTokens 10}. That is exactly the usage the first try recorded at line 110, so it cannot tell the retry's own count from the first try's count carried over, which is the incident's usage failure. Checked by mutation: with usage pinned by session id for good, as before the fix, and the intermediate view step (lines 122-123) removed, this test passes. The refusal rests only on the view assertion at line 123, plus test 2. If the retry wrote a different number of responses (say 3), the recorded end would refuse the carried-over count by itself.

reviews.summary: I reviewed 00e301b and 741350c, and the fix is correct. What runner.ts keeps for a finished session now belongs to one attempt (the row's name, its session id and the registry's start), and the runner reads again once the transcript's mtime is past the read. That holds for both closeouts and usage, domain.ts is untouched, and nothing outside the package changed. The new tests fail against the pre-fix runner and against a runner with the mtime check removed. The engine suite and typecheck pass (215 of 218 tests, 0 failures). I found two small problems, neither worth another round: the README and a code comment state an unproven cause as fact, and one test assertion can't tell the retry's usage from the first try's.

findings.what: `idRefusal` accepts dots, and the files keyed by a run's id are that id plus a suffix, so a dotted id can name another run's files. Take `wf rm r-xyz.json`, which is what `ls ~/.agent-workflows/runs` or tab completion there gives. `runFile('r-xyz.json')` is `runs/r-xyz.json.json`, which does not exist, so `forget` takes the no-record path (runner.ts:1364). `removeKeyed` then removes `path.join(runsDir(), id)` (runner.ts:1483), which is `runs/r-xyz.json`: the real run's record. The line reads `no such run — ... removed runs/r-xyz.json` and exits 0. No check runs first: nothing about in-flight tasks, work due, asks or runs waiting on it. If r-xyz has a session running, that session keeps going in a worktree nothing reads; `wf cancel r-xyz` now says no such run; its worktrees and branches are orphaned; and a child waiting on it reads `(no such run)` for ever. `wf rm r-xyz.cancelled` deletes a cancelled run's `.cancelled`, so the run reads as live and the tick files its next step, which features.md itself names as the danger. `wf rm r-xyz.asks` drops a person's unspent asks. `runId` only mints `[a-z0-9-]` ids, and no id in the machine's store has a dot, so refusing anything else costs nothing. Add a test: `wf rm <id>.json`, `<id>.cancelled` and `<id>.asks` against a live run are refused with exit 2, and its record, cancellation and asks stay.

Minor, and not the reason for another round. The README says a pass halfway through a run that is being forgotten writes nothing back, but `collectArtifacts` runs before any `mayFile` or `rewriteRun` guard and makes its target with `mkdirSync(..., { recursive: true })` (runner.ts:1810). Case: a `--no-worktree` run whose last step has no check stays in `handOffDue` on every pass. If the tick listed the run before `wf rm` and reaches it after, the workspace (the repository itself) is still there, the copies in `runs/<id>/artifacts/<step>/` are gone, and the pass copies the closeout's workspace artifacts back. That recreates `runs/<id>/` with no record. `wf ls` does not show it, and a second `wf rm <id>` sweeps it. Either skip collection when the record no longer exists, or mention it under 'What it leaves'.

reviews.summary: Reviewed the whole `wf rm` diff with a focus on round 2's three fixes: re-reading the run before filing, reporting a hand-off git refused, and holding detached worktrees. All three hold up, and typecheck and the workflows suite pass (429 passed, 1 skipped). One real hole is left: `idRefusal` accepts dots, so `wf rm <id>.json` (or `.cancelled`, `.asks`) takes the no-record path and deletes another run's record, cancellation or asks without any of the refusals. There is also one minor case where a stale pass recreates `runs/<id>/`.

findings.what: The text still says 'a run that files steps from a plan is still §2 below'. Moving item 1 to Shipped renumbered 'A run that grows steps from a plan' to '## 1.' (line 1599), so there is no §2 any more and a reader following the reference finds nothing. It should read §1.

It says 'The cancel-then-`wf rm` case is closed: all a pass does after its last re-read is `e.file`'. The code does more than that. In the try loop, after `mayFile()` (runner.ts:1083) the pass still awaits `e.view(taskId)`, `refusalOf(...)` and `e.view(asking.taskId)`, then runs `fs.mkdirSync(artifactsDir, { recursive: true })` (runner.ts:1098), and only then calls `e.file`. The check loop is the same: `mayFile()` at runner.ts:1190, then `await e.view` and two recursive mkdirs (runner.ts:1196-1200). Example: a pass reads a run that has a try or check due, and a scripted `wf cancel x && wf rm x` finishes in that gap. The pass then recreates `runs/<id>/artifacts/<step>/` with no record and files a session into a worktree that is gone. The gap is a few milliseconds of journal reads, so this is unlikely in practice. Either move the `mayFile()` check to just before the mkdir and `e.file`, or soften the sentence.

reviews.summary: I found nothing worth another round. Both round-2 fixes hold. `idRefusal` now takes only ids shaped like the ones `runId` makes, and a pure test plus a store test make it refuse `<id>.json`, `<id>.cancelled` and `<id>.asks`. With no record, the check-log sweep now leaves alone logs whose names start with another stored run's id. A pass that read a `--no-worktree` run before `wf rm` no longer hands it off or collects its files, and a store test covers that. I read the whole diff against c1fed2a. agent-workflows passes (433 tests, 432 passed, 1 skipped by design), api passes 137 with `--force`, and typecheck is clean. I also checked that every record in the machine's store fits the id alphabet and the `worktrees/<id>/<step>` and `wf/<id>/<step>` layout that `wf rm` looks for. Two small points are left for a person: a section reference in features.md that the renumbering broke, and a claim in features.md about a race that the code does not quite back up.

findings.what: On a cancelled run, `forgetRefusal` never judges a ready step, and `forget` never looks for a step a pass has filed but not yet written down (runner.ts:1324-1326 looks for checks, tries and rounds only). Simplest case: `wf start`, then while the first pass is cutting implement's worktree (`npm ci` can take a minute) the person types `wf cancel` then `wf rm`. `cancel` sees nothing running and marks the run. `wf rm` sees a cancelled run with nothing running, removes the worktree and the record. The pass then calls `e.file` with a working directory that is gone (runner.ts:1186), and `rewriteRun` quietly writes nothing. The session is now on the engine's board, and no pass will ever stop it: every pass stops a cancelled run's work, but only a run it can find a record for. `npm ci` can also create `worktrees/<id>/<step>/node_modules` again, the disk `wf rm` was meant to free. The brief says a ready step counts because a pass may be filing it at that moment, and a step being filed has not settled. features.md mentions the gap, but says only that nothing reads the task, not that nothing stops it. Possible fix: on a cancelled run, look up the task id each would-be-ready step would get (`stepTaskId(run, name, tryOf(run, name))`) and count it as running if the engine has it, as the existing check/try/round lookups do. And in `advance`, just before each `e.file`, re-check that the record still exists and the run is not cancelled. Add a store test that holds a pass between cutting the worktree and filing while `cancel` and `forget` run.

If the hand-off commit fails, `handOff` hides why: a failing pre-commit hook (husky/lint-staged on a failed step's broken code) or `commit.gpgsign=true` with no agent is enough. `git worktree remove` then refuses the dirty tree, so the work is safe, but the run's line only passes on git's first stderr line: `fatal: '<wt>' contains modified or untracked files, use --force to delete it`. The only advice the person gets is the one command that deletes the failed step's uncommitted work. The line never says the commit was tried and refused, or why, and `wf rm` again repeats the same thing. It should say the hand-off could not commit (with the commit's own error) and give a safe next step, such as committing in the worktree yourself. Or the forget hand-off could commit with `--no-verify -c commit.gpgsign=false`, since its only job is to keep the work. No store test has a hand-off commit that fails.

A worktree whose HEAD is detached (git lists it with no `branch`) is handed off and removed like any other. The commit is made on the detached HEAD, and `git worktree remove` then leaves it, plus any commits the session made there, on no branch and unreachable. The line still says `committed what <step> left uncommitted as abc1234` (without `on <branch>`), which reads as if the work was kept. How a step ends up there: its session ran `git rebase`, `git bisect` or `git checkout <sha>` and was stopped or hit its deadline, exactly the failed or stopped work the brief says lives only in the worktree. Such a worktree should hold the run and be named, as a locked one is, unless its HEAD is already on a branch.

reviews.summary: Reviewed `wf rm` against the brief: the pure judgement in run.ts, `forget` and the write-back guard in runner.ts, the CLI, and the README and features.md. It covers the brief and the tests are real (package suite 424 tests, 423 passing and 1 skipped; typecheck clean). Three gaps remain, all ways to lose work or leave a run's session running with nothing watching it: forgetting a run cancelled while a pass is still filing its step, a hand-off commit that git refuses, and a worktree whose HEAD is not on a branch.

findings.what: The `git` helper calls `execFileSync` without `stdio`, so Node copies git's stderr to the process's own stderr as well as putting it in the error message. Before this change only a person's `wf start` reached it, once. Now `startQueued` (runner.ts:1244, via `startFromInbox` → `start` → `makeWorkspace`) retries a card that failed without a refusal on every pass. A queued card whose `repo:` is a folder with no git prints `fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git` on `wf up`'s terminal every 4 seconds, with no card name, for as long as it holds the queue. That contradicts the README's claim that `wf up` says it once. Running `node --test --test-name-pattern="fails without a refusal" test/queue-store.test.ts` shows four such lines for four passes. The test (queue-store.test.ts:563-577) only captures `console.log`, so it passes. Passing `stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'pipe']` to the helper keeps git's words in the error without the echo; a test that captures `process.stderr.write` over those passes would pin it.

`wf up` skips a queue line marked `again`, and `again` is judged against the try saved in `$WF_ROOT/queue/<name>.json` (runner.ts:1251), not against what this `wf up` process has printed. So a `wf up` started, or restarted, after the failure was written never names the card holding the queue: its first pass already reads `again: true`. queue-store.test.ts:574 pins exactly that, since its two `wf up` passes print nothing about `no-git-a1b2`, not even once. A person restarting the daemon to see why cards stopped starting gets no line about it; only `wf inbox` shows it. Remembering the last printed line in the `up` loop is presentation, not a decision the tick carries between passes, so it would not break the level-triggered rule.

reviews.summary: The four items do what was asked, and all three fixes from the last round are in with tests. The agent-workflows tests pass without turbo's cache (485 pass, 1 skipped) and typecheck is green. The run cap, item 31 and the queue are consistent across `wf tick`, `wf ls` and `wf decide`. Two small findings on the path where a queued card's start fails without a refusal: git's error is printed on every pass, and a daemon started after the failure never mentions the card. Both are worth a person's attention but not another round.

findings.what: `runSlots` (and `decide`, through it) reads the cap from the environment of the process that calls it, not the daemon's. The README's own example sets it only on the daemon: `WF_MAX_CONCURRENT=4 WF_MAX_RUNS=2 wf up` (README.md:1264). In that setup, `wf ls` in another shell reads a cap of 0, so `heldRuns` returns nothing. A run the daemon is holding then reads plain `waiting`, and `wf decide` on it says `still running: implement` instead of the slot line. A shell with a different `WF_MAX_RUNS` prints a wrong `n of m`. The queue-store tests set `process.env.WF_MAX_RUNS` for the whole test process, so none of them catches this. The record's `slotHeldAt`, which the daemon writes, is never consulted by `wf ls`. Possible fixes: have the daemon record the cap it runs with somewhere `wf ls` reads, or at least word a run with `slotHeldAt` as held. Either needs a test that runs `wf ls` without the variable set.

A queued card whose `repo:` folder has been deleted is never tried and never mentioned on `wf up`. `parseInboxCard` refuses it ('names no directory'), so the catch here builds a listing entry with no `queued`. `queueOrder` and `nextQueued` then leave it out, and `startQueued` never reaches it. `wf up` logs nothing about it, and `wf inbox` shows only the parse error, without the card's place in the queue. The brief says a start refused because 'the repository [is] gone' is named on `wf up`'s line and in `wf inbox`, and README.md:1318 claims the same. Only the workflow-gone case is tested. One fix: read `queued:` without the directory check, so the card stays in the queue order and `startFromInbox` refuses it by name. Add a test that deletes a queued card's `repo:` folder.

For a person to confirm. The brief asked for 'one try per pass'; this code tries a refused card once and then never again until the card's text changes. The catch also takes any error as a lasting refusal, not just the package's exit-2 refusals: a one-off git failure while `start()` sets up the workspace, or a `wf up` briefly run from the wrong folder for a card with no `repo:`, sticks until someone runs `--off` and queues the card again. Putting the missing workflow back does not un-stick it (features.md lists this as left). It also adds a store folder, `$WF_ROOT/queue/`, and a stored refusal that decides later passes, which the brief did not ask for. The reasons are sound: no log spam every 4s, and cards behind a refused one still get their turn. At least consider retrying errors that don't carry exitCode 2 on the next pass.

reviews.summary: I reviewed all four commits against e776cc0 and read the new code closely. Typecheck passes, and so does the full suite: engine 299, workflows 480 with 1 skipped, api 152, web 181. Items 28 and 31 look right, and their tests fail if the fix is broken. Two gaps are worth another round: the run cap is read from the environment of whichever command is running, so a `wf ls` in another shell doesn't see the cap `wf up` was started with; and a queued card whose `repo:` folder is gone is skipped silently. A third point, that a refused card is never retried, is a design choice for a person to confirm.

findings.what: The link refusal tells the person to "copy what it points at over it, cp --remove-destination", which is GNU coreutils only. On macOS — the filesystem family the same function's case-insensitivity fix is written for — `cp` has no long options at all, so following the message gives `cp: illegal option -- -` and the person is left with a refusal whose named fix does not run. Either drop the flag from the sentence or name a portable pair (`rm <file> && cp <target> <file>`). The same sentence is duplicated in test/write-workflow.test.ts:263, so a fix touches both.

reviews.summary: Reviewed the four commits against the brief and ran both gates: `npx turbo run test --force` green in all four packages (agent-workflows 593 / 591 passed / 2 skipped, api 202, web 248, agent-engine 340 / 331 / 9 — the counts features.md claims, matched exactly) and `npm run typecheck` clean. All four items do what was asked, each with a test that fails without it, and round 1's two findings are settled rather than worked around: the `up` loop keys on what this daemon printed (so a pass at a full cap, which reads no queue at all, does not spend the daemon's one chance to name the card), and the write-order test asserts every removal before the write as a partition rather than readdir's sequence. One finding: the refusal for a linked step file names `cp --remove-destination`, a GNU-only flag, on a refusal whose own docstring is about macOS and Windows filesystems. Declared leftovers in features.md — two steps whose names differ only by case, the api's now-redundant `utimesSync` — are honestly stated with reasons that hold, so I did not re-raise them.

findings.what: `first = false` runs on every pass, including one that never read the queue: when the cap on runs in flight is reached, `tick` skips `startQueued` altogether (runner.ts:2111) and `queue` is undefined, and the up loop prints nothing about the queue (it prints no `slotWord`, unlike `wf tick`). So with WF_MAX_RUNS=1 and a run in flight, restarting `wf up` after a queued card's start failed spends its first pass in silence; when the slot frees, the card's failure matches the QueueTry the previous daemon wrote, `again` is true, and the daemon never names the card — the very case this change is for, and the one a person restarts the daemon to see. Clear `first` only once a queue line has been printed, or remember per-daemon what it has said (card + why) rather than leaning on the store's `again`; a test at a cap of 1 pins it.

The order is asserted as ['removed review.md', 'removed ship.md', 'wrote REVIEW.md'], but `removed` (runner.ts:1106) keeps `fs.readdirSync`'s order, which is neither sorted nor guaranteed — hash order on ext4 and APFS. On a machine or a copy that lists ship.md before review.md the test fails though the rule it pins holds, and this is the only test that proves the rule where the filesystem tells case apart. Assert that every removal precedes the first write (or sort the removal entries) instead of the exact sequence.

reviews.summary: Reviewed the five commits against 2ea2128: all four leftovers are implemented in packages/agent-workflows only, and each is pinned by a test that fails without the fix (the stderr test mocks process.stderr.write, which is precisely how execFileSync echoes a child's stderr, so it really refuses the un-fixed helper; the case-rename test rightly skips on a case-sensitive filesystem and the fs-call-order test carries the rule here). Forced suite green — npx turbo run test --force, 4/4 tasks, agent-workflows 590 pass/2 skipped, api 202 — and npm run typecheck 4/4. Two findings: wf up still goes silent about a stuck card when its first pass never reached the queue (cap full), and the new order assertion depends on readdir order.

findings.what: With CELL_HEIGHT at 260 the diamond's span reads `rows: 2`, which is what line 208 already asserts for the fan-out, so the one assertion that distinguished a three-lane graph from a two-lane one no longer does. A `spanOf` regression that read only the first two lanes' y (max 174 instead of 324) yields ceil((174+150)/260) = 2 and passes both lines; at 220 the diamond line caught it (3 vs 2). The comment above still says "the diamond's three, which reach further down", which nothing now measures. A fixture whose lanes reach past two cells — or a wider fan asserted at rows: 3 — would put the distinction back. Low value: the CELL_HEIGHT − ROW_HEIGHT boundary assertions two lines below still pin the row arithmetic exactly.

reviews.summary: Reviewed all eleven commits against 3cf06a0 and ran the suite: `npm run typecheck` and `npx turbo run test --force` are green (317/9 engine, 202 api, workflows and web pass), and I read the e2e PNGs implement left in the run's artifacts — the floor lays out clear of itself in both themes. All four of round 1's findings are genuinely answered: the schema being written is now put back by comparing what the file holds rather than by which writes returned, the status-null banner no longer contradicts its own message, the inbox keys refusals by file, and the CELL_HEIGHT won't-fix holds on its stated reason. I found one small coverage loss, not worth another round; I wrote nothing into the workspace.

findings.what: The file the write fails on is not put back, and `fs.writeFileSync` truncates before it writes. `written.push(before[i]!)` runs only after a successful write, so a failure *during* a write — ENOSPC, EDQUOT, EIO, the disk-full case the commit is about — leaves that schema on disk empty or half-written and restores everything except it, while the doc at line 266 says the save is left "no more written than a refusal does". EACCES and EISDIR fail at open and so happen to be safe, which is why both tests pass. Pushing `before[i]` before the write closes it: restoring a file the write never touched is a no-op.

260 is tuned to the e2e's seed, not to what the card can draw. `RunNode` renders one `<li>` per need (`needsOf` flat-maps every step, each `line-clamp-2`), plus a `waiting` word of up to 2 lines and a steps list that wraps, so the height is unbounded in the data. The measured 233 already includes a 2-line ask (`palette asks: Warm colours for the dark theme, or cool ones?` at ~58 chars in a 288px card), leaving about 27px of headroom — roughly one and a half lines. A run whose two parallel steps both ask, or sign off blocked (a diamond does this), draws ~270 and reaches over the card beneath it again, exactly as at 220. Nothing catches it: `expectClearOfEachOther` measures only the seeded floor, where one card has one need. Either the card needs a cap on what it draws (the second option in the brief) or the comment should say plainly that the constant holds for the cards the board draws today.

`status === null` is not only a lost fetch. `build()` (lib/api.ts:678) also throws a status-null `BuildRefusal` when the api answers 2xx without what it wrote, so the banner's head reads "the api did not answer" directly above a message that reads "PUT … answered 200 OK without what it wrote" — two contradictory sentences in one box. The offer to read the folder again is right for that case; only the wording is wrong ("the api did not say what it wrote" covers both).

In the very collision item 3 now seeds into the e2e — `notes.md` beside a stray `notes` — a refusal is matched to a line by name, so a failed Remove of the card renders the red refusal box twice: once under the card and once under the stray file, which has no Remove button of its own and cannot be refused anything (`refusalFor` at routes/inbox.tsx:40 keys by name too). Pre-existing, not introduced by this change, but reachable only through the case the change is about; matching on `entry.file` instead would fix both.

reviews.summary: Reviewed the five commits against 3cf06a0: the builder's schema restore, the save banner's 4xx/5xx split, inbox `hasPage`, and the Factory's cell height. `npx turbo run test --force` and `npm run typecheck` are green from the root (api 201 tests, the new read-only refusal ran rather than skipping); I could not run build or e2e from this step, so those claims in RESPONSE.md are unverified here. Four findings, none of them a break in what the suite covers: one hole left in the restore the first commit claims, one constant tuned to the e2e's tallest card, and two smaller wording/adjacent bugs.

Reviewed all four items against the code and ran the suite: `npx turbo run test --force` green from the root (engine 340 tests, 331 pass, 9 AE_LIVE skipped) and `npm run typecheck` green. The busy-quiet rule traces correctly through `closedOut` and `decide` (no false `unsigned`, the inherited-statement guard is judged against the registry's start, which is strictly later than the journal's), the nudge is pinned word for word, and both new tests for items 3 and 4 genuinely fail without their rule — the reversed listing defeats the stable sort, and without `poolsOf`'s `claude-bg` branch `cc` becomes a pool of its own. Round 1's two findings are properly fixed: `keptRead` now takes `keep` from its caller with the old default intact, and the pin is still dropped by mtime.

findings.what: `Sighting.quietMs`'s doc still defines the field as "How long the session has been quiet — working, not busy, nothing written". After this change the claude runner sets `quietMs` on a sighting it reports with `busy: true` (runner.ts:1121), and that combination is exactly what now ends an attempt. This is the only place the engine states the runner↔engine contract — `decide` reads the field at domain.ts:481 and `closedOut` (engine.ts:111) still refuses to act on a busy statement — so the next reader, or the next runner written against this type, is told the one case that matters cannot happen. `QUIESCENT_AFTER_MS`'s doc at runner.ts:172 has the same stale clause ("How long `working` + not busy + nothing written must hold"), though the same constant is now also the busy rule's floor. The README and the `claudeOps` header both got the second rule; these two did not.

For a busy session whose transcript has been cold for the floor, `statementOf` runs on every pass: `keptRead` pins a read only when `FINAL.has(s.state)`, and this session's state is `working`, so it falls through to `read()` each time — a full `fs.readFile` of the transcript plus `jsonl.split('\n')` and a per-line scan, of a file the code's own comment (runner.ts:249) calls "tens of megabytes". The case is not rare: any tool call longer than 90s — `npm ci`, a build, this repo's own suite — leaves the session busy with a cold transcript for its whole length, so under `wf up`'s few-second tick that is the same multi-megabyte read and parse repeated for minutes, always returning the same answer. Previously a busy session cost nothing at all. The read is safely pinnable precisely because the condition being tested is that the transcript has not been written: the mtime + `MTIME_SLOP_MS` machinery `keptRead` already has would give one read per cold period instead of one per pass. If the cost is accepted instead, that is a judgement worth stating where the comment at runner.ts:1073 promises a busy session "costs its transcript's mtime and nothing more".

reviews.summary: Reviewed the four commits against the brief: all four items are implemented as asked, `npm test` (forced, uncached) and `npm run typecheck` are green from the root, and each item's test does fail without its rule (verified by reading the fixtures and the sort/pool logic rather than by editing). Two findings, both small: the `Sighting.quietMs` contract doc in domain.ts now contradicts the runner it documents, and the busy branch re-reads the whole transcript on every pass for the length of any tool call longer than the floor.

findings.what: The comment says review is "Read-only by machinery, not by its brief": under dontAsk, any Bash command `.claude/settings.json` doesn't allow is denied. workflows/dev/README.md:12 goes further: review "cannot write, by machinery rather than by its brief". dev-build/review.md repeats the comment. It isn't true. `.claude/settings.json` allows `Bash(npm run build)` and `Bash(npm run e2e)`, and the brief two paragraphs down says both write into the workspace. So review can run either one without a prompt, and only the brief stops it. If it does, the build rewrites apps/web/src/routeTree.gen.ts and the e2e writes `.e2e/`, and the run commits those files under review's name. CLAUDE.md's rule is that prose is not a constraint, and this text claims a guard that doesn't cover those two commands. In this change's own files, the fix is to say that only the brief keeps review away from build and e2e: settings.json has to allow them because implement's session runs them. Making it true takes a per-step allow list or a settings change. That is outside the files this change owns, so a person should decide.

reviews.summary: Round 1's three fixes hold. POST /api/runs refuses a start by content-type (415), Sec-Fetch-Site (403) and Host (403), each before reading the body. The api listens on 127.0.0.1 only. Hidden folders are neither listed nor startable. startRun has unit tests for a start, each refusal and a 201 with no id. The rest meets the request: the loader skips READMEs, the dev, dev-build and ui folders are there, both routes and the Workflows page work, and the screenshots look right in both themes. `npm test` (api 64/64) and `npm run typecheck` pass, though turbo replayed both from cache. One wording issue is left for a person: a README and a comment say the reviewer can't write "by machinery", but `.claude/settings.json` allows `npm run build` and `npm run e2e`.

findings.what: POST /api/runs accepts a request from any other website. `c.req.json()` parses the body whatever its content-type, and nothing checks `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site`. So any page the person visits can run `fetch('http://localhost:8787/api/runs', {method: 'POST', body: '{"workflow":"dev","brief":"…"}'})`. That body is sent as text/plain, so the browser does not ask the server first, and the api answers 201 and writes a run record with the attacker's brief. The same works through vite's `/api` proxy on :5173. On top of that, `apps/api/src/main.ts:14` calls `serve` with no hostname, so the api listens on every network interface and anyone on the network can POST directly. Once `wf up` is running, it files that run and a Claude session (`--permission-mode auto`) acts on the attacker's text in the person's repository. GETs were already exposed, but this is the first write. Fix: answer 415 unless the content-type is `application/json`, refuse a cross-site `Origin`/`Sec-Fetch-Site`, and bind to 127.0.0.1. Add a test that sends a text/plain POST and a cross-site POST, expects both refused, and checks no record is written.

`foldersIn` lists every directory, hidden ones included. If a person keeps `~/.agent-workflows/workflows/` in git (a natural thing for personal workflows), `.git` shows up as a red card: `.git has no .md steps in it`. An editor folder such as `.vscode` under `<repo>/workflows/` does the same, and the 404 message lists them among the workflows there are. findings.what: `Engine.transcript` refuses any `after` that does not match `readTranscript`'s `<offset>.<16 hex>` format, for every harness. But `PromiseRunner.transcript` is documented to take "a cursor this method returned", so a custom runner owns its cursor. Say one returns `{ events, cursor: 'page-2' }` or `'42'`: the next `engine.transcript(id, 'page-2')` is rejected with exitCode 2 ("`page-2` is not a cursor a transcript read gave"), and a board can never get past that harness's first read. Such a runner is also later handed the engine's own START cursor (`0.e3b0c442…`), which it never returned. The test at test/transcript.test.ts:443 hides this by giving its PromiseRunner a cursor already in the file format (`'7.0123456789abcdef'`). Either leave the format check to the built-in file reader (still mapped to exitCode 2) and pass a PromiseRunner's cursor through untouched, or state and enforce the format in the `PromiseRunner` contract. Add a test with a cursor in a runner's own format.

`transcript` calls the task's harness's `observe` directly, with no fallback. `logs` goes through `composite`, which turns a failed `observe` into an empty map (runner-composite.ts:35-38) and so falls back to the journal's `last.nativeId`. Concretely: take a finished `claude` task whose session id is in the journal. If `claude agents --all --json` fails or prints something that is not JSON (the contention CLAUDE.md records for the api tests), `engine.logs(id)` still reads the transcript but `engine.transcript(id)` rejects, even though the file read never needed the registry. Every poll also spawns `claude agents`, and claudeOps' second pass re-reads the full transcript (closeout and usage) of every idle `ae/` session on the machine, on each call. When `observe` fails, fall back to the journal's id as `logs` does, and consider skipping `observe` when the last attempt has ended and its `nativeId` is already in the journal. No test covers a failing `observe`.

findings.what: `lessonGlobs` and `groupOf` (line 131) use the base's `workspaces` strings as globs from the repository root, exactly as written, but npm also accepts `./packages/*` and `packages/**`. Every package's changes then land in one `packages` group, and the lesson glob `./packages/*/docs/` never matches `packages/x/docs/features.md`. A branch that wrote exactly that lesson prints `lesson  nothing written where the next agent reads`. With `packages/**`, the lesson glob becomes `packages/**/docs/`, which matches `packages/x/src/docs/a.md`: the false lesson round 1 fixed comes back. This repo's `packages/*` and `apps/*` are unaffected. The fix is to strip a leading `./` when the workspaces are read, plus a radius test with `['./packages/*']` that makes the lesson line refuse. `**` can at least be noted in `wf decide --help`.

findings.what: `LESSON` uses `**/docs/`, which matches a `docs/` folder at any depth. The request asked for a package's `docs/`. reviews.summary: Round 2 review: all three fixes hold. The step page and its api route moved to /workflows/<repo|yours>/<workflow>/<step>, with no `steps/` address left anywhere. A folder in the inbox no longer gets a link. The 404 names only the .md files and matches DELETE's sentence. `npx turbo run test --force` and `npm run typecheck` pass (the typecheck was a turbo cache hit), and I looked at the round-2 screenshots from the e2e. One gap is left, too rare to need another round: a stray file with no extension that has the same name as a card opens the card's page.

findings.what: An inbox entry that doesn't read as a card now links to `/inbox/<entry.name>`. For a folder inside the inbox, the package lists the entry as `sub/` (`inboxFiles` in runner.ts adds a trailing `/`), so the link goes to `/inbox/sub%2F`. `GET /api/inbox/:name` then refuses `sub/` with a 400 via `inboxNameRefusal`, because the name contains a slash. The page shows "Could not load this card: `sub/` is not a card's name … Give the name wf inbox lists", even though the Inbox page just listed that exact name. Fix: don't link an entry whose `file` ends in `/`, or give it a page. No api or e2e test puts a folder in the inbox, so nothing catches this.

The 404 message builds "Its cards are:" from every entry the listing has, including files that aren't `.md` and folders. With `notes.txt` and `sub/` in the inbox, `GET /api/inbox/nope` says "Its cards are: …, notes.txt, sub/". The package's own message for the same case (`startFromInbox` → `inboxCards()`) keeps only `.md` files. Also, `.filter((e) => e !== entry)` does nothing on the `!entry` path. No test covers a 404 in an inbox that holds something other than cards.

The operator's approval (the plan's retry answer) set the step page at `/workflows/<repo|yours>/<workflow>/<step>`. The build puts it at `/workflows/<from>/<workflow>/steps/<step>` and gives the reason only in features.md ("as a run's step is at /runs/<id>/steps/<step>"). Every link the Workflows page makes, the e2e route and the api path follow the changed address. Either move it to the approved address, or have a person confirm the change: it contradicts an explicit answer.

reviews.summary: I reviewed the full diff against the base commit. The test suite passes in all 4 packages (run with `--force`), typecheck is clean, and the implementer's screenshots of the card page and the step page render correctly. The markdown component does what was asked: raw HTML stays text, `javascript:` links are refused, and each refusal has a test that makes it refuse. I found one real bug and two smaller problems: a folder in the inbox gets a title link to a page that can only show an error; the "not found" message lists files that aren't cards as cards; and the step page's address differs from the one the operator approved.

findings.what: No test checks that `closeoutAsked` reads the *last* attempt's reason. The fake engine in store.test.ts only ever makes one attempt, so changing `attempts.at(-1)` to `attempts.some(...)` would still pass every test. The difference is real because a step can declare `maxAttempts` (workflow.ts:205, passed on at runner.ts:1013). Example: with `maxAttempts: 2`, attempt 1 goes quiet unsigned, the engine nudges, and attempt 2 then ends `lost` or `harness`, so the task settles `failed`. Today that correctly reads `failed`. Under the `some` version it would read `unsigned`: the run would be called `blocked` and the brief would say 'gave no closeout' when the nudged session actually broke. The code is right; a two-attempt case in the store test would lock it in.

reviews.summary: Reviewed d5023a3, a single commit with a plain message and no trailers. It does what was asked: a failed task whose last attempt ended `unsigned` now reads `unsigned` again, so the run is `blocked`, the step is listed as waiting on you, and a retry brief says it gave no closeout. A task that failed for any other reason, or was stopped, reads as before, and `stepStatus` is still pure. The two touched test files pass when run directly (219 of 219); `npm test` and `npm run typecheck` exit 0, but turbo replayed both from its cache. I found no correctness bug, only one small test gap, which doesn't need another round.

findings.what: This assertion checks almost nothing. `get` parses the response with `res.json()`, so no value in `shown` is the same object as `first`. `shown.indexOf(first)` is therefore -1, and `shown.slice(-1)` checks only the last value. So 'from the first answer on, never nothing' is never really tested: if the section went blank for a moment between the placeholder and the new answer, the test would still pass. The regression that matters (no placeholder) is still caught by the `meanwhile` assertion above it. To check what it claims, find the first index where the data is deep-equal to `first` (e.g. `shown.findIndex((d) => d !== undefined)`).

`touchedSummary` adds up `+a −r` over every branch it reads, but a follower in its own worktree starts from its parent's branch (`runner.ts:600`). Take implement → review-a and review-b, each in its own worktree. Both are result branches, and `git diff base...review-x` includes implement's changes on both. So the Factory card shows implement's lines twice, e.g. `+1958` for 979 lines of work. The package count is deduplicated with a Set; the line counts are not. `wf decide` prints each branch on its own line and never adds them up, so the card disagrees with the CLI here. The seed and the tests only cover the one-branch case.

reviews.summary: Both round-one fixes hold. `decisionStamp` treats a filed step whose status is still changing as one word, and `keepPreviousData` keeps the last decision on screen. It can't show one run's decision on another run's page, because `Run` is keyed by `run.id`. The new r-d6/r-d7 test reaches the running-while-waiting-on-you branch and shows that a blocked step beside a live sibling reads as `failed`. The commands match `cli.ts:321-331`; `npm test` and `npm run typecheck` are green (turbo cache hits); and the implement step's screenshots show the Decide section between the banner and the canvas, the card's `touched 2 packages · +435 −1`, and the loop page's unread branch. Two small findings remain, neither worth another round.

findings.what: `decisionStamp` keys the decision on each step's `status` word. For a step still running, `listing` (run.ts:1275) passes through the engine's phase, which flips between polls with no change to the decision: `running (working)` ↔ `working (quiescent)` when the harness's `busy` changes, and `starting`, `between attempts`. Take a run the board treats as decidable while a step is live: a fan-out with implement blocked (the run is `running` with waitingOnYou) and tokens still working, or a `failed` run whose sibling still runs. Each flip is a new query key, so the page and the open Factory card ask `/decision` again: an engine observation per task, then `git diff`. That breaks 'fetched once, not polled'. `decisionQuery` has no `placeholderData: keepPreviousData` (StepInspector.tsx:198 uses it for the same reason), so `data` is undefined during each re-read. `Decide` (Decide.tsx:25) and `TouchedLine` (RunNode.tsx:128) render null until it lands: the section vanishes and the canvas jumps up under the cursor, then back down. The stamp test (test/decide.test.ts:67-73) only checks that the key moves when a word changes. Nothing checks that it holds while a live step's engine word changes and nothing settles. Key on what the decision depends on (task ids and settled words, with every in-flight word treated as one), and/or keep the previous data.

No test covers the api's own branch for a run `assess` calls `running` while a step waits on a person, which the request counts as decidable. Past line 583, `decision()` returns kind `running`, so the result branches come from `terminalSteps` (lines 595-597) instead of `d.branches`, and `commandsOf` returns []. decision.test.ts seeds only a finished run, a running run with nobody waited on, unreadable branches, cancelled and shipped. A break in that branch would go unnoticed: a throw, the wrong branches, or `{ running: true }` returned for it (which would leave the page's Decide section and the Factory's `touched …` line blank for exactly the runs waiting on you). Add a route test on a fan-out: one step signed off blocked, a sibling still spawned. It should assert `touched` and `lesson` are read off the terminal steps' branches and that `commands` is empty.

reviews.summary: I reviewed the route, the Decide section, the used/cost rows, the Factory card line and the tests. The suite and typecheck pass (turbo replayed cached runs), and implement's e2e screenshots of the run, loop and Factory pages look right. Nothing in packages/ or S2's files was touched. Two findings are worth a round: the decision's cache key moves on every change in a running step's engine word, and the "running, but a step waits on you" path the request names has no api test.

findings.what: Only a `readable` event clears the retry error, and a new server stream starts with `failing = false`, so it never sends one. Case: a read fails mid-stream, the page shows "Could not read task … Reading it again every second.", then the connection drops (for example the api restarts). The EventSource reconnects and the api's read before opening the stream succeeds. Events flow again, but the red error stays under the header until the task settles. The fix is small: a stream that opened at all means that read worked, so clearing `error` on the EventSource `open` event (or on any `transcript` event) is correct. No test covers a reconnect while the error is showing.

reviews.summary: Round 2 holds: nothing needs another round. The four fixes are in: the NUL byte is gone, every waiting call in a parallel batch shows as running, a failed stream read is retried instead of ending the stream (tested for both ways it can end), and both session photos (light and dark) now start at the prompt with the fold opened. `npm test` (59 api tests) and `npm run typecheck` pass. I checked that the installed @hono/node-server 2.1.1 cancels the response when a tab closes, so the stream stops polling. The "won't fix" on the two `claude agents` calls a second per open stream is backed by a measurement and a sound reason, so I did not raise it again. One minor issue remains: after a reconnect, the retry error can stay on screen while events keep arriving (low severity, raised without asking for another round).

findings.what: `keyOf` joins `kind` and `id` with a literal NUL byte in the source (cat -v shows `${event.kind}^@${event.id}`). Because of that byte, git treats the whole file as binary: `git diff --numstat c6ce655` gives `-	-` and `git diff` prints `Bin 0 -> 11342 bytes`. So the person who merges, and any PR view, sees none of the fold's ~250 lines. Later edits or a conflicting merge of this file also get no line diff and no textual 3-way merge. Write the escape `'�'` instead, or use a printable separator: `kind` is a closed set with no ':', so `${kind}:${id}` is unambiguous.

While live, a call without a result counts as running only if it is the fold's last call (`last && inner === lastCall`; `stateOf` at :79). Claude Code writes parallel calls as consecutive tool_use lines, and their results come after all of them. So while a batch runs (say three Bash calls from one message), every call but the last shows 'No result' with a grey circle in the opened fold. That looks like a dropped call until its result lands. In a fold that is last while the session is live, every call without a result is still running, so pass `running = live && last` to each call. Add a test: a live fold with two pending calls shows both as `running`.

One failed read on the stream sends `unreadable` and returns. The client (`useStepTranscript.ts:56`) then closes the EventSource for good. Any rejection triggers this: `e.view` failing on a journal read (EMFILE under load, say) or `e.transcript` failing to open the file for a moment. The page then drops 'following live' and says the conversation 'could not be read any further' while the session keeps running, until someone reloads. The rest of the design is level-triggered, and the next second's read would most likely succeed. Nothing tests this branch, and nothing tests the /transcript route's 502 either, although /log has a 502 test. Simplest fix: close the stream without `settled`, so the EventSource reconnects from Last-Event-ID on its own. Or keep polling. Add a test that makes one read fail and checks that following resumes.

The session page is a full-height scroller that opens at its end, so `fullPage` (visit.ts:38) captures only the last 800 px. Neither session-light.png nor session-dark.png shows the prompt bubble, the opened thought, or the fold line 'Ran 3 commands, searched code, read 3 files · 1 failed'. That line is the main thing the brief asked for, and nobody has seen it in either theme. The Activity tab in run-*.png also shows only the tail (Edit, a system line, the closeout). The DOM assertions pass, but the screenshots do not show what they checked. Scroll the conversation to the top at the end of the page's `expect`, or photograph the fold, before the shot.

Every read calls `e.view` only to learn `settled`. That call checks every harness: `claude agents --all --json`, plus the Claude runner's pass over the closeout and usage of every idle `ae/` session. Then `e.transcript` runs `claude agents` again for an attempt still in flight. So each open session page or Activity tab on a running Claude step spawns the registry twice a second, plus the idle-session reads. packages/agent-engine/docs/open-issues.md expects one call per poll (~300 ms) and says nobody has measured this. `settled` is also in the journal: `engine.feed`, with a cursor the stream holds after one initial view, reports it without querying any harness. Not worth a round on its own; at least record the cost in the closeout so it reaches open-issues.

reviews.summary: The routes, the fold, the session page, the Activity tab and the tests that were asked for are all there. I reran the new tests without turbo's cache: 8 api transcript tests and 18 web tests pass, and the apps/web typecheck passes. Root `npm test` and typecheck came from turbo's cache, for the same inputs. No Claude Code web link was added, and the registry row the engine parses has no URL field. Five findings: transcript.ts contains a NUL byte, so git shows the file as binary; parallel calls read "No result" while they run; one failed poll on the stream ends live following for good, with no test; the session screenshots never show the fold line; and each open stream runs `claude agents` twice a second.

findings.what: A run whose ending the pass will NOT file still claims the checkout, and holds every other run's ending behind a session that does not exist. `mainClaim` counts a claim on `a.ready.includes(ending.name)`, but `advance` files `ready` only when `runReady(run, shipped) && admitted` (runner.ts:1625) — two gates `mainClaim` never asks. Both apply only to a run with nothing filed, which is reachable exactly when the ending is a root: a one-step `workspace: main` folder, which `validateMainWorkspace` allows (its `beside` list is empty) and `stepsToStart` refuses only under `--no-worktree`. Concretely: start such a merge-only folder `--after` the work run (or with `WF_MAX_RUNS` full), approve its ship — `approvalRefusal` allows it, since `waitsAtGate` sees no `after` — and it is now `ready` with an approval time, so `heldCheckouts` hands it the checkout as the oldest word. Run B files nothing (`wf decide` returns early on `waitWord`/`slotWord`), while every other run at its ending's gate reads `waiting on the checkout (B's ship has it)` on `wf ls` and `wf decide` says `the next tick files ship once B's ship has settled` — of a ship that has never been filed and will not be until B's parent ships or a slot frees. This is the rule `mainClaim`'s own docstring states ("only where the pass would in fact file it… an ending that will not be filed does not hold another run's") and the same rule as the lost-task case. Note `hasStarted(run)` alone is the wrong fix: it would open the reverse hole, since for a one-step folder `hasStarted` is false exactly while the ending is waiting to be filed, so such a run would then be filed into a checkout another run's ship is merging in. The decline branch of this predicate has no store test either — the pure `heldCheckouts` test covers `at: undefined`, but nothing at the store level shows a run declining to claim.

reviews.summary: Reviewed the six commits against the six findings: all six are implemented where the finding is, each refusal has a test that makes it refuse on `err.message` at shipped defaults, and the order rules are pinned by fixtures given the opposite order. `npx turbo run test --force` from the root three times — runs 2 and 3 fully green, run 1 had store.test.ts and the api's transcript.test.ts both cancelled on the event loop, which I could not reproduce and read as contention, not the change; typecheck clean. One finding: `mainClaim` counts a claim on the checkout without asking the two questions `advance` asks before it files a root, so a run the pass will never file can take the checkout and starve every other run's ending on that repository. Two items stay open outside what this step owns: the board's `commandsOf` (the seventh finding, recorded in features.md), and `apps/api` never passing `checkout` to `listing`/`decision` nor the asks to `gateLines`, so the Factory shows a held ending as plain `waiting` and still offers `wf approve` in the un-held window — the `waiting on …` wording was chosen for a reader that cannot yet see it.

findings.what: A try the checkout holds is filtered out of `retry`, so the `status.set(r.step, 'running')` on the next line never runs and the ending keeps a status that stops followers — `assess` then calls the whole run `failed`. Take the case the change's own test builds (ship.test.ts, "a try of an ending step waits for the checkout…"): ship signed off blocked, the person typed `wf retry <run> ship --message "…"`, another run's ship has the checkout. `wf decide <run>` no longer prints "still running: ship" — `decision` never reaches its running branch, so the ended screen prints "BLOCKED, waiting on you: ship" and then offers "ship: blocked. Continue its session, told what happened:  wf retry <run> ship" (retryLines) plus the same command again under ship's `needs` (answerLines) — a command `retryRefusal` refuses with "try 2 of ship is already asked for". At the same moment `wf ls` of that run lists nobody in `waitingOnYou` and says "try 2 asked (--nudge) — waiting on the checkout": the two screens disagree about whether anything waits on the person. `advance` also returns `status: 'failed'` and `inFlight: false` (slotNeed counts `retry`), so a run merely queued behind another's ending stops counting against the cap on runs in flight and a queued run is admitted in its place. Keeping the held step 'running' in the status map while leaving it out of `retry` gives the first-filing behaviour to the try too: `decision`'s `waitsForCheckout` (run.ts:2983) would say "still running: ship", and cli.ts:742's `retrying.filter((r) => !(heldOut && r.step === ending?.name))` — written for exactly that shape and unreachable today for the same reason — would become live.

Nothing records that the board cannot see the hold, though the same document records the `commandsOf` gap it does leave. `checkoutHold` is async and lives in runner.ts; apps/api/src/app.ts:722 calls `listing(...)` with no `checkout` and app.ts:730/1319 call `assess`/`decision` without one, so on the Factory an approved ending held behind another run's ship draws the plain word `waiting` — indistinguishable from an approved ending the next tick will file — and a held try draws a run still running with a try due. The careful choice of `waiting on the checkout (…)` over `waiting for …`, made so `stepState` draws it as a step with nothing filed, reaches no board today. A person watching the board sees a run stop for minutes with no word for why; `wf ls` is the only place that says it.

reviews.summary: Reviewed the change against 96c719b: the checkout hold (heldCheckouts/checkoutHold/mainClaim), the ending step's artifacts contract, and the four refusal/word fixes. Suite and typecheck green from the root, measured with `npx turbo run test --force` (agent-workflows 588 · api 202 · web 248 · agent-engine 340, 0 failures). Two findings: `assess` dropping a held try makes the run read as failed, so `wf decide` and `wf ls` disagree in that window; and the board cannot see the hold at all, which is not recorded under features.md's *What it leaves*. The seventh finding from the last review — the board's `commandsOf` (apps/api/src/app.ts) offering `git merge` for a run whose ending merges — is still open, correctly left alone and recorded in features.md.

findings.what: A retried ending escapes the hold, which is the collision item 1 exists to stop. `checkoutHold` returns undefined as soon as the run's own ending has a taskId, and `assess` applies the hold only to `ready` (run.ts:258) — `retriesDue` and `advance`'s retry loop (runner.ts:1622, filing with `cwd: record.workspace`, which is `run.repo`) consult nothing. Concretely: run A's ship signs off blocked after its check refused (the path test/ship.test.ts:332 already plays), so the checkout frees and run B's approved ship is filed and is merging; a person then types `wf retry A ship --message "…"` — allowed, since `retryable` gives ['nudge','fresh'] to a blocked settled step and `retryRefusal` returns null — and the next tick files A's ship try 2 in the same checkout. Both sessions read `git status --porcelain`, both `git merge --no-ff --no-commit`, and the loser's `git merge --abort` throws away the winner's staged merge. No test covers a retried ending against a held checkout, and README.md (`while a workspace: main task of any run on the same repository is unsettled, another is not filed`) and docs/features.md:2805 both state the rule in a form the code does not keep.

A cancelled run's ending task holds nothing while it is still in flight: the loop skips every `other.cancelledAt` run before it looks at the task's phase. `wf cancel` only asks the engine to stop the session; between that request and the engine settling the task as `stopped`, the ship agent is still mid `git merge` in the checkout, and the next tick files another run's approved ship into the same directory — two agents merging at once, the case the hold is for. The doc comment justifies only the lost-task (`unknown`) case, where a run nobody can stop must not hold the checkout for ever; a cancelled run's task settles on its own within a tick or two, so the same reasoning does not cover it.

The new status word is one the board cannot name: `stepState` (apps/web/src/lib/status.ts:55) matches only `waiting`, `waiting on …` and `pending`, so `waiting for the checkout (r-1's ship has it)` falls through to the `working` default at line 58 — the Factory draws a blue chip whose hover text reads "working: its session is running" for a step with no task filed at all. Fixing status.ts is outside what this step owns, but the word is not: `waitWord`'s `waiting on …` prefix would land in the right branch. Worth knowing that `slotWord` (`waiting for a run slot (…)`) already reads as `working` on the board for the same reason, so this is a second instance rather than a new kind of problem.

The `unheld` adjustment added to `decision`'s `statusOf` has no test that fails without it, so it could be deleted and the suite would stay green. In the window the new test reads (test/run.test.ts:3509) ship is neither 'checking' nor 'running' whether `statusOf` calls it 'awaiting approval' or 'waiting', and `assess` already drops it from `ready` through its own `unheld`, so `decision(...).waiting` is `['review']` either way; `statusOf` is read again only in the non-running branch (`awaitingApproval`, `overBudget`), which this window cannot reach, since a try due makes `assess`'s overall status 'running'. The `gateLines` half of item 4 is properly pinned (the `{}` and the restored line); the `decision` half needs a fixture the change actually moves — a run whose status is not 'running' while the ending is un-held — or an assertion on `awaitingApproval`.

reviews.summary: Reviewed the nine commits against the six findings: items 2–6 land as asked, with refusals pinned on `err.message` and every command they name honoured at that moment, and item 1's two store tests fail without the rule (the second run's approval written older, so the ordering is the rule's). `npx turbo run test --force` and `npm run typecheck` are green from the root (agent-workflows 583, 582 passed / 1 skipped). Item 1 is incomplete: the hold is wired into `assess`'s `ready` only, so a retried ending — `wf retry <run> ship` after one that signed off blocked — is still filed into a checkout another run's ship is working in, which the README and features.md now claim cannot happen. The seventh finding, the board's `commandsOf` offering `git merge` (apps/api/src/app.ts), is untouched and still open, as it should be.

Round 2: implement's fix answers last round's finding, and I found nothing else worth another round. A run from before collection now reads files named from the workspace off its branch, whether or not its worktree is still there. A file whose copy was refused is still named `not collected`. Their reason for dropping the "hand-off is past" condition holds: a task the engine lost never hands off. agent-workflows ran uncached: 369 tests, 368 passed and 1 skipped. The root `npm test && npm run typecheck` exited 0, all four packages replayed from turbo's cache.

findings.what: `workspaceArtifact` returns 'not collected' whenever the file is still in the workspace and not in the step's files directory, and it checks the branch only when the workspace has nothing there. No code removes a worktree, so every run whose steps handed off before this change still has its workspace. After the merge, `wf decide` on such a run prints `!! declared and not collected: RESPONSE.md — in the workspace, and not in <dir>` for every file a step named from the workspace root, the brief's own example. The old code found those files on the branch and printed nothing. The warning never clears: those steps are past hand-off (check filed, or a later step in the workspace), so `collectArtifacts` never runs for them. Fix: if hand-off is past and nothing now blocks the copy (a link or non-directory on the way in the files directory, or something that is not a file in its place, as `plainDirectoriesTo`/`lstatOf` check), check the branch as before. The link test in store.test.ts still expects 'not collected' and would keep passing. No test covers a record from before collection with its worktree still present; add one: a step settled, its check already on the record, `RESPONSE.md` committed on the branch and present in the workspace, and `missingArtifacts` returns [].

reviews.summary: Reviewed the six commits (radius globs, step order, --input, workspace artifacts collected, stale ask, wf start on a card). The agent-workflows tests pass (367, 1 skipped) and typecheck is clean across the repo. One bug is worth a round: `wf decide` now warns 'not collected' for every file a step named from its workspace on runs handed off before this change, because the branch is only checked when the workspace has nothing there.

findings.what: This change now draws the Decide section for a run whose only row is a harness-blocked step's asked try. Above that row, the Answer heading (line 103) and the frame's intro (lines 42-43) still say "the next tick files it", and the intro says "copy one to run it yourself" when there are no commands. The row beneath says "stopping its blocked session, then the tick files it". So a person reads, on one screen, that the next tick files a try the tick will not file: it stops the session first. You can see it in held-asked-light.png and held-asked-dark.png. Word the heading so it does not promise the filing (for example, "and the tick files it"), or leave the promise to the row.

Docs that now say the opposite of what ships. Item 10 still says "the board's POST does not yet (item 23)", item 23 (line 971) is not marked done, and the §4b Settled bullet (lines 783-784) still says the board shows "the two commands that continue it". In packages/, which this step may not edit, the same stale claim is in four places: `retry()`'s doc comment (packages/agent-workflows/src/runner.ts:1207-1209) says the board calls it without the option and apps/api's tests hold a 409; packages/agent-workflows/README.md:614-615 says the board's POST still refuses; docs/features.md:696-700 and 771-777 say the same; and test comments at test/run.test.ts:874 and test/store.test.ts:1819 say "the board's POST, today". The next person to read any of these will think the board still refuses a harness-blocked step. If the plan's concurrent owner allows it, the plan lines are the merger's to fix (CLAUDE.md, When you miss); the package lines need a packages step.

reviews.summary: I found no correctness bugs. The api's retry route now passes `{ stopBlocked: true }` and answers 202 with `stopFirst`, and `StepAsked` carries `stopFirst` too. A step that is still working is still refused in `retryRefusal`'s words, with nothing written and no session stopped. On the run page, the banner's Continue replaces the two commands, and the Decide section is drawn once the try is asked. The api and web tests pass, and so does typecheck (both replayed from turbo's cache of implement's run). Implement's e2e log shows every page passing in both themes, and I read the `held` screenshots. What's left is text: docs outside apps that now say the board refuses, and one Decide heading that contradicts the new row.

All five fixes from round 1 hold up against the code. The board no longer offers a Continue that the package refuses: `retry()` refuses a harness-blocked step as "still running", and the api test pins that refusal. The two commands the banner gives instead match the engine: a stop request settles the task `stopped`, and `retryable` then offers a nudge. Only a run's detail reads the session's last line, and a test counts the `claude agents` calls (1 for the list, 1+1+3 for the detail).
